title: He Has Risen: The Empty Tomb
summary: Early on the first day of the week three women come to anoint Jesus' body and find the great stone rolled away. A young man in white tells them that Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified, has risen, and sends them to tell the disciples and Peter that he is going ahead of them into Galilee; they flee in fear and say nothing to anyone. Verses 9 to 20, absent from the earliest complete manuscripts, describe appearances of the risen Jesus, his commission to preach the gospel to all creation, and his ascension.
story:
Mark's story ends where it has been heading since the first passion prediction: after three days the Son of Man will rise (8:31, 9:31, 10:34). The women who watched the crucifixion from a distance (15:40-41) and saw where the body was laid (15:47) are the first to hear the news. They are the only people in Mark present at all three events, the death, the burial, and the empty tomb, and so the chain of witness is unbroken. The message they receive restores the disciples who fled, naming Peter, who denied Jesus three times, in particular. The promise that Jesus goes ahead of them into Galilee repeats his word on the way to Gethsemane (14:28) and sends them back to where the story began, beside the sea where they were first called, now to follow him again.

The chapter also poses the most debated textual question in the New Testament. In the two oldest complete manuscripts the book ends at verse 8, with the women running from the tomb and saying nothing because they were afraid. Most later manuscripts continue with verses 9 to 20, a summary of resurrection appearances, a commission, and the ascension. Whether Mark meant to end at verse 8, whether his ending was lost, or whether verses 9 to 20 are his, the resurrection is not a footnote to his Gospel but its goal. Acts and the letters of the New Testament are what happened when the disciples went to Galilee and saw him.
historical:
The Sabbath ended at sunset on Saturday, and buying and selling were forbidden until then, so the women bought spices that evening and came at first light on Sunday. The Mishnah allows a body to be washed and anointed even on the Sabbath (m. Shabbat 23:5), but the spices had to be bought first. The day they came became the day of Christian worship. Paul tells the Corinthians to set aside gifts ‘on the first day of every week’ (1 Corinthians 16:2), Acts describes the church gathering on that day to break bread (Acts 20:7), and Revelation calls it ‘the Lord's day’ (Revelation 1:10). The Didache (14.1), Ignatius of Antioch around 110 (Magnesians 9.1), and Justin Martyr around 155 (First Apology 67) all speak of Christians gathering on the Lord's day or the day of the sun because it was the day Christ rose, and the Roman governor Pliny, around 112, reported to Trajan that Christians met on a fixed day before dawn to sing a hymn to Christ as to a god (Letters 10.96).

The women are named, and the named witnesses matter. In the Jewish and Roman world women's testimony was often given less weight than men's; Josephus says that under the law the testimony of women was not to be accepted (Antiquities 4.219), and the pagan critic Celsus, writing around 175, dismissed the resurrection as resting on the word of a half-frantic woman (Origen, Against Celsus 2.55). Many historians, including skeptical ones, conclude that a story invented to persuade would hardly have made women its first witnesses, and all four Gospels agree that they were. Rival explanations began early. Matthew reports that the priests paid the guards to say the disciples had stolen the body (Matthew 28:11-15), and Justin Martyr, around 160, says Jewish teachers were still spreading that account in his day (Dialogue with Trypho 108). A marble slab bought in Nazareth in 1878 and now in Paris, the so-called Nazareth Inscription, records an imperial edict threatening death to anyone who disturbs tombs; it was once linked to the Christian story, but a 2020 study of its marble traced the stone to the island of Kos, which makes any connection with Jesus' tomb very doubtful.

The ending of Mark is a question of textual history, the study of how the New Testament was copied and handed down. Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, both copied in the fourth century, end the book at verse 8. In Sinaiticus the leaves carrying Mark 14:54 to Luke 1:56 were rewritten by one of the manuscript's own scribes, and the replacement still stops at verse 8; in Vaticanus the scribe left a full column blank after verse 8, the only such gap in its New Testament. Eusebius of Caesarea, early in the fourth century, reported in his Questions to Marinus that the accurate copies, nearly all of them, ended there, and his system of Gospel cross-references (the Eusebian canons) stops at verse 8; a note in several medieval manuscripts of the family known as Family 1 still says so. Jerome repeated the report in his Letter 120 to Hedibia (about 407), yet kept the longer ending in the Latin Vulgate. On the other side, most later Greek manuscripts contain verses 9 to 20, among them Codex Alexandrinus, Codex Ephraemi, Codex Bezae, and Codex Washingtonianus, all of the fifth century or near it; Irenaeus, around 180, quotes verse 19 as coming toward the end of Mark's Gospel (Against Heresies 3.10.5); and Tatian wove the verses into his Diatessaron, a single narrative made from the four Gospels, about the same time.
cultural:
Jews did not embalm the dead as Egyptians did. They washed the body, wrapped it in linen, and applied spices and perfumed oils as an act of love and to lessen the odor of decay, and family and friends could return to the tomb in the first days after burial. The women came expecting a corpse and worried, reasonably, about the stone. Wealthy families' tombs were cut into the soft limestone around Jerusalem, with a low entrance and one or more chambers inside, where the body was laid on a bench or in a niche; after about a year the bones were gathered into an ossuary. Most such tombs were closed with a squared stone block; a minority, generally the more elaborate, had a round stone rolled in a channel, and Amos Kloner's survey (Biblical Archaeology Review, 1999) found few of these from Jesus' time. Either way the stone was heavy, and Mark adds that it was very large.

The young man sitting on the right in a white robe is presented as a heavenly messenger. White garments mark heavenly origin, as at the transfiguration (9:3), and Jewish writings of the period often describe angels as young men: two splendid young men appear to Heliodorus in the temple in 2 Maccabees 3:26, and Josephus describes the angel who appeared to Samson's mother as a handsome youth (Antiquities 5.277). Fear, trembling, and amazement are the normal human response in Scripture to God's direct action, from Sinai (Exodus 19:16) to the stilling of the storm (4:41) and the transfiguration (9:6). They are not simply unbelief.

The announcement ‘He has risen’ landed in a world where resurrection already had a meaning. By Jesus' day many Jews, following Daniel 12:2 and books like 2 Maccabees 7, hoped that God would raise the righteous dead bodily at the end of the age; the Pharisees taught it and the Sadducees denied it (Mark 12:18-27; Acts 23:8). The second blessing of the synagogue's central prayer, the Amidah, praises God who gives life to the dead, and the Mishnah denies a share in the world to come to anyone who says the resurrection of the dead is not taught in the Torah (m. Sanhedrin 10:1). What no one expected was the resurrection of one man in the middle of history, ahead of everyone else. Greeks and Romans, for their part, mostly regarded bodily resurrection as impossible or undesirable, as the Athenians' laughter in Acts 17:32 shows. Galilee, to which the disciples are sent, was home: the lake, the boats, and the villages where they had first heard Jesus' call.
literary:
Verses 1 to 8 are brief and carefully built. The women's anxious question about the stone (verse 3) is answered before they arrive, and Mark adds, as he often does, a short explanatory clause with ‘for’ at the end: it was very large. The young man's words reverse the darkness of chapter 15 in three terse statements without connecting words, ‘He has risen; He is not here; see the place’, and pair the resurrection with the crucifixion: the one they seek is ‘Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified’. The commission names the disciples ‘and Peter’ and ties the future to Jesus' own word, ‘just as He told you’.

The last line is startling: “And in their fear they did not say a word to anyone.” Throughout Mark people told to be silent have talked (1:44-45, 7:36); now people told to talk are silent. If the book ends here, the final Greek word is gar, ‘for’, in the clause ‘for they were afraid’. That is an unusual way to end a sentence and a very unusual way to end a book, but not an impossible one. Pieter W. van der Horst (Journal of Theological Studies, 1972) pointed to a treatise of the philosopher Plotinus that ends with gar, and Septuagint sentences such as Genesis 18:15 end the same way. Readers who think Mark ended here, such as R. H. Lightfoot (1950), J. Lee Magness (Sense and Absence, 1986), Andrew Lincoln (Journal of Biblical Literature, 1989), and the literary critic Frank Kermode (The Genesis of Secrecy, 1979), see an ending that leaves the reader to answer the call the women failed to carry out, trusting the promise of verse 7, which the existence of the Gospel shows was kept. Others find such an ending too abrupt for any ancient book and conclude that the last page was lost.

Verses 9 to 20 read differently. They restart the morning as if verses 1 to 8 had not happened, introduce Mary Magdalene as if for the first time though she has just been named three times, and use a cluster of words and phrases found nowhere else in Mark. Their content gathers material found in other books: the appearance to Mary Magdalene (John 20:11-18), the two walking in the country (Luke 24:13-35), the rebuke and commission of the Eleven (Luke 24:36-49, Matthew 28:16-20), speaking in new tongues (Acts 2:4, 10:46), a snakebite survived (Acts 28:3-6), healing by the laying on of hands (Acts 28:8), and the ascension (Luke 24:51, Acts 1:9-11). They are built around one theme: again and again the disciples refuse to believe (verses 11, 13, 14), until the risen Lord rebukes their unbelief and sends them anyway. James Kelhoffer (Miracle and Mission, 2000) argued that the passage was composed in the first half of the second century as a summary drawn from the other Gospels and Acts.

outline.t: The women at the empty tomb
Jesus appears to Mary Magdalene (longer ending)
Jesus appears to two in the country
Jesus appears to the Eleven and sends them out
The ascension and the disciples' preaching

doctrines.note: The church confesses, as a first-order article of faith, that Jesus was bodily raised from the dead on the third day. The young man joins identity and event: “You are looking for Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified. He has risen!” (verse 6). The one who was crucified is the one who is risen, and the place where his body lay is empty. This is not a metaphor for his influence or the disciples' renewed courage but an event, the firstfruits of the resurrection promised to all who belong to him (1 Corinthians 15:20).

The message goes to “His disciples and Peter” (verse 7), all of whom fled and one of whom denied Jesus with oaths. Restoration begins with the risen Lord's initiative, before any of them has said a word, and the way back for failed followers is an invitation before it is a demand. The longer ending, too, has Jesus rebuke the Eleven's unbelief and then commission them.

The women leave “trembling and bewildered” (verse 8). Mark does not present their fear simply as unbelief but as the awe of creatures before God's direct act, the same response that met the stilling of the storm (4:41) and the transfiguration (9:6). Whether or not the book ends here, fear is the first human response to the resurrection, and it is not the last.

The women are sent to tell the disciples, and in the longer ending the risen Jesus sends the Eleven: “Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature” (verse 15). The story of Jesus does not end with his followers watching; it continues in their going, which Mark's Gospel had anticipated in 13:10 and 14:9.

The ending of Mark shows how the church received its Scriptures. Verses 9 to 20 were read in the churches' worship for centuries and are printed in nearly every Bible, while most scholars judge them to be an early addition. Christians of every tradition agree on what the passage says; they differ on whether Mark wrote it, and most now build no doctrine or practice on these verses alone.

words.note: Egeirō, to raise or to rise, used of waking from sleep, getting up, and rising from the dead. It occurs about 144 times in the New Testament and nineteen in Mark. The young man's announcement is ēgerthē, passive in form. It can be read as a divine passive, ‘He has been raised’, with God as the one who acted; but this verb's passive forms are often intransitive, simply ‘He has risen’, as the BSB renders it, so the divine passive is possible rather than required. The New Testament speaks both of Jesus rising and of God raising him. The same verb described Jesus raising Simon's mother-in-law (1:31) and Jairus's daughter (5:41).

Proagō, to go before, lead the way. It occurs about twenty times in the New Testament and five in Mark. Jesus walked ahead of his frightened disciples on the road to Jerusalem (10:32), promised to go ahead of them into Galilee after rising (14:28), and now ‘He is going ahead of you’ (verse 7), in the present tense, already on the way. It is a shepherd's word: the risen Lord does not wait for his scattered flock to find its way back; he leads them.

Ekthambeomai, to be utterly astonished or alarmed. It occurs only four times in the New Testament, all in Mark: of the crowd who saw Jesus come down from the mountain (9:15), of Jesus himself in Gethsemane, ‘deeply troubled’ (14:33), and twice here, of the women's alarm and the young man's ‘Do not be alarmed’ (verses 5 and 6). The word that described the Son's anguish before the cross now describes the women's shock at its reversal.

Tromos, trembling. It occurs five times in the New Testament, here and four times in Paul, always joined with fear: Paul came to Corinth ‘in weakness and fear, and with much trembling’ (1 Corinthians 2:3) and tells the Philippians to work out their salvation ‘with fear and trembling’ (Philippians 2:12). The phrase comes from the Greek Old Testament, where it describes the dread that falls on the nations at God's acts (Exodus 15:16, Psalm 2:11). The women stand in that line.

Ekstasis, astonishment, amazement, literally a standing outside oneself. It occurs seven times in the New Testament, twice in Mark: at the raising of Jairus's daughter, when the family was overcome with ‘great amazement’ (5:42), and here at the empty tomb (verse 8). In Acts it can mean a trance or vision (Acts 10:10, 22:17). BDAG gives both senses, a state of being so overwhelmed that one is beside oneself, and a trance. Mark uses it for the response to God raising the dead.

Phobeomai, to fear, be afraid, revere. It occurs about ninety-five times in the New Testament and twelve in Mark. It can describe terror, reverence, or both, and the standard lexicons treat the range from being frightened to showing reverential respect. In Mark the disciples ‘were terrified’ after the storm was stilled (4:41) and afraid to ask about his death (9:32); verse 8 ends with it, ephobounto gar, ‘for they were afraid’. The imperfect tense describes a continuing state rather than a single moment of fright.

Apisteō, to refuse to believe, disbelieve. It occurs eight times in the New Testament, twice in the longer ending (verses 11 and 16), and Luke uses it for the disciples who ‘did not believe’ the women's report (Luke 24:11). Verse 14 uses the related noun apistia for the Eleven's unbelief, the word Mark used for Nazareth's unbelief (6:6). The early church did not hide the fact that its first leaders doubted, and the risen Jesus rebukes their hardness of heart before he sends them.

Analambanō, to take up. It occurs thirteen times in the New Testament, eight of them in Acts, and only in verse 19 in Mark. In the Greek Old Testament it is the verb for Elijah being taken up into heaven (2 Kings 2:11), and Acts uses it for Jesus' ascension (Acts 1:2, 1:11, 1:22), as does the early hymn of 1 Timothy 3:16. Joined to the phrase ‘sat down at the right hand of God’, from Psalm 110:1, it tells in one sentence of Jesus' exaltation to reign beside the Father.

christ:
The chapter shows that the crucified Jesus is alive. The young man's words hold the two together: “You are looking for Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified. He has risen!” (verse 6). The perfect participle for ‘crucified’ presents the crucifixion as a completed act whose mark remains; the risen Lord is still the crucified one, as Paul preaches ‘Christ crucified’ (1 Corinthians 1:23) and John shows the risen Jesus with the marks of the nails (John 20:27). His death was real, and so is his resurrection. The church has always confessed his bodily resurrection as the event on which its faith stands or falls (1 Corinthians 15:14-17), and Paul's list of witnesses in 1 Corinthians 15:3-8, handed on to him within a few years of the events, shows that the appearances were proclaimed from the start.

The resurrection vindicates everything Mark has said about Jesus from the first line. He is the Christ and the Son of God; his three predictions that the Son of Man would rise after three days have come true to the letter; and his claim before the high priest that he would be seen at the right hand of Power is now under way. The rejected stone of Psalm 118, which he quoted against the temple leaders (12:10-11), has become the cornerstone. His death was not defeat but the ransom he came to give (10:45), and God's raising him is the Father's verdict on the Son whom the world condemned.

The risen Jesus is also the shepherd who gathers his scattered flock. He had applied Zechariah 13:7 to himself, ‘I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered’, and in the same breath promised to go ahead of them into Galilee (14:27-28). Now the promise is renewed, with Peter's name added. In the longer ending he is taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God, the place Psalm 110:1 gave to David's Lord and that Jesus claimed at his trial, and from there he works with his people as they preach, confirming the word. That is the story Acts goes on to tell.
interpretation:
The ending of Mark was discussed almost as soon as the church began comparing its Gospels. Eusebius's Questions to Marinus, early in the fourth century, took up a reader's question about how Mark 16:9, ‘early on the first day of the week’, could agree with Matthew's ‘late on the Sabbath’, and answered first that the accurate copies ended at verse 8 and then that, if the passage was accepted, the two could be reconciled by punctuation. Jerome repeated the first answer to Hedibia (Letter 120, about 407) while keeping the verses in the Vulgate, and quoted part of the saying later called the Freer Logion from Greek copies (Against the Pelagians 2.15). The verses nevertheless became part of the church's reading. Gregory the Great preached on verses 14 to 20 in Rome on Ascension Day 591 (Homilies on the Gospels 29), and the Council of Trent (1546), in accepting the books of the Vulgate with all their parts, was generally understood to include them.

Modern textual criticism reopened the question. John Burgon's The Last Twelve Verses of the Gospel According to S. Mark (1871) defended the verses as Mark's against the growing consensus, and in the same decade Westcott and Hort's Greek New Testament (1881) printed them in double brackets. The English Revised Version of 1881 set them apart with a note that the two oldest Greek manuscripts omit them, and almost every modern translation has followed with a note or brackets. William Farmer (The Last Twelve Verses of Mark, 1974), Maurice Robinson, and Nicholas Lunn (The Original Ending of Mark, 2014) have defended their authenticity; Bruce Metzger's Textual Commentary and James Kelhoffer (Miracle and Mission, 2000) argued against it; and Perspectives on the Ending of Mark (2008), edited by David Alan Black, sets out four views, from Daniel Wallace's case for an intended ending at verse 8, to Keith Elliott's for a lost ending, to Robinson's and Black's for the longer ending, with a response by Darrell Bock. Literary readers, from R. H. Lightfoot (1950) to Frank Kermode (1979) and Andrew Lincoln (1989), turned the ending at verse 8 from an embarrassment into a subject of study.

The resurrection itself has been the subject of the modern world's sharpest debates about the Gospels. Hermann Samuel Reimarus, in fragments published by Lessing in 1778, argued that the disciples stole the body; Gerd Lüdemann (The Resurrection of Jesus, 1994) argued that the appearances were visions born of grief and guilt, beginning with Peter; and Dale Allison (Resurrecting Jesus, 2005), writing as a historian, concluded that the tomb was probably found empty and that people did see Jesus after his death, while leaving the final explanation open. N. T. Wright's The Resurrection of the Son of God (2003) argued at length that only a bodily resurrection explains the rise of the Christian belief. The Orthodox Jewish scholar Pinchas Lapide (The Resurrection of Jesus: A Jewish Perspective, 1977, English 1983) accepted the resurrection as a historical event while denying that it made Jesus the Messiah. Verses 17 and 18 had a painful modern afterlife: serpent handling as worship began in the Appalachian holiness movement with George Went Hensley around 1910, and it has cost lives, including Hensley's own in 1955.

The chapter is at the center of Easter worship. In Year B of the Revised Common Lectionary, verses 1 to 8 are read at the Easter Vigil and may be read on Easter Day; the Roman lectionary reads verses 1 to 7 at the Easter Vigil in Year B and verses 15 to 20 on the Ascension in Year B. In the Orthodox churches the Sunday resurrection Gospels read at Matins run in an eleven-week cycle, of which the second is Mark 16:1-8 and the third Mark 16:9-20, and on the Sunday of the Myrrh-bearing Women, the second Sunday after Pascha, the Divine Liturgy reads Mark 15:43 to 16:8. In art the women at the tomb are among the oldest Easter subjects, long before painters attempted the resurrection itself, which no Gospel describes; Duccio's panel of the three Marys at the tomb, painted for the Maestà altarpiece in Siena (1308 to 1311), shows them drawing back in fear before the angel seated on the stone.
text:
The ending of Mark is the largest textual question in the New Testament, and English Bibles present it in different ways.

The short text ends at verse 8. Its witnesses are Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (both fourth century), the Sinaitic Syriac, one Sahidic Coptic manuscript, and the oldest Armenian and Georgian manuscripts, supported by Eusebius's and Jerome's reports that the accurate or nearly all Greek copies ended there and by the Eusebian canons, which stop at verse 8. The longer ending, verses 9 to 20, is found in the great majority of Greek manuscripts, including Codex Alexandrinus (A), Codex Ephraemi (C), Codex Bezae (D), Codex Washingtonianus (W), and Codex Koridethi (Θ), in most Latin, Syriac, and Coptic copies, and in the Byzantine text behind the King James Version. It was known by the late second century to Irenaeus and Tatian, and perhaps earlier to Justin Martyr (First Apology 45).

A shorter ending also circulated. In its usual form it says that the women reported briefly to Peter and those with him all they had been told, and that afterward Jesus himself sent out through them, from east to west, the sacred and imperishable proclamation of eternal salvation. The Old Latin Codex Bobiensis (k), of the late fourth or early fifth century, is the only manuscript that has the shorter ending alone after verse 8. Several Greek manuscripts give both endings, the shorter first and then verses 9 to 20: Codex Regius (L, eighth century), Codex Athous Lavrensis (Ψ), the fragments 083 and 099, and the minuscule 579, some with a note explaining that the longer ending is also current; many Ethiopic manuscripts do the same. No one defends the shorter ending as Mark's.

Codex Washingtonianus (W), a manuscript of the late fourth or fifth century now in the Smithsonian's Freer Gallery in Washington, adds a further dialogue after verse 14, the Freer Logion, in which the disciples blame Satan for the unbelief of the age and Christ answers that the term of Satan's power is fulfilled. Jerome knew part of it; no other Greek manuscript has it.

Modern English Bibles handle this evidence in different ways. The King James Version and New King James print verses 9 to 20 without brackets (the NKJV with a note). The ESV, NIV, NASB, CSB, and BSB print them with brackets, a heading, or a note that the earliest manuscripts end at verse 8, and some, such as the NRSV, also print the shorter ending. Within the longer ending, some manuscripts lack ‘new’ in verse 17 and ‘with their hands’ in verse 18, and the closing ‘Amen’ appears only in later copies.

teach.big: The crucified Jesus has been raised and goes ahead of his failed followers, calling them back to follow him, so that the story of the gospel does not end in the silence of fear but continues wherever his people go and tell.

outline.t: Love brings the women to the tomb expecting a corpse, and the obstacle they fear has already been moved; God acts before his people arrive.
The heart of the gospel in three short sentences: the crucified Jesus is risen, he is not here, see the place; the resurrection is an event, and the risen one is still the crucified one.
The first word of the risen Lord to his failed friends is not a rebuke but an invitation, with Peter named, and he is already going ahead of them.
Fear and silence are the first human response to the resurrection; if Mark ends here, the ending hands the reader the task the women left undone.
In the longer ending, the first witness is a woman once possessed by seven demons, and the disciples will not believe her; faith in the resurrection came against expectation.
Two more witnesses report and are not believed; the church's first leaders were not credulous.
The risen Lord rebukes unbelief and then sends the unbelievers into all the world with the gospel, promising that signs will accompany the preaching; his protection is a promise, not a dare.
Jesus is taken up and sits at God's right hand, and from there he works with his messengers, confirming the word: the mission is his before it is theirs.

teach.pitfalls:
The first pitfall is to preach verses 9 to 20 without telling the congregation what nearly every modern Bible's note says. Honesty about the text builds trust, and it is possible to read the passage as an ancient summary of the resurrection faith while building nothing on it alone. The opposite error is to dismiss the passage as worthless; it has been read in the church for most of its history and agrees in substance with the other Gospels and Acts. A second, more serious misuse is to treat verse 18 as a command to handle snakes or drink poison. The verse promises protection; it does not command testing God (Matthew 4:7), and the practice has cost lives. A third is to use verse 16 on its own to settle the relation between baptism and salvation; Christians read it differently, and it belongs to the disputed ending.

With verses 1 to 8, avoid scolding the women for their fear and silence as if they were simply faithless. Mark presents their fear as the awe of people who have met the power of God, and the reader knows the message got through. Avoid, too, turning the empty tomb into a purely spiritual symbol of renewal. Mark's point is that the body is gone and the crucified one is risen. Finally, do not let the ending debate crowd out the good news of verse 7: the first message of Easter in Mark is addressed to people who failed, and to Peter by name.
teach.pastoral: This chapter speaks to grief, to failure, and to fear. The women came to do the last loving thing for a body, and many who hear it will remember standing at a grave; the news that the tomb is empty is the Christian hope for their dead, and it should be spoken gently and plainly. Verse 7 speaks to those who believe they have failed God beyond repair, as Peter did; the message came to him by name before he had done anything to earn it. For the anxious and the doubting, the chapter is honest that the first response to Easter was fear, silence, and, in the longer ending, repeated disbelief, and that Jesus did not abandon those who struggled to believe. And for anyone harmed by a church that demanded proof of faith through dangerous signs, it is worth saying clearly that verse 18 never commanded them.

hard.q: Did Mark's Gospel originally end at 16:8, and how should readers treat verses 9 to 20?
hard.a:
The objection to the longer ending is strong. The two oldest complete manuscripts end at verse 8, Eusebius and Jerome said that the accurate or nearly all Greek copies they knew ended there, and the verses differ from the rest of Mark in vocabulary and style, restart the story awkwardly, and gather material found in Luke, John, and Acts. On this basis most textual scholars, including many who hold a high view of Scripture's inspiration, such as Bruce Metzger and Daniel Wallace, conclude that verses 9 to 20 were added early by another hand. The defenders of the longer ending answer with the other side of the evidence. John Burgon (1871), William Farmer (1974), Maurice Robinson, David Alan Black, and Nicholas Lunn (2014) point out that the verses are found in the great majority of Greek, Latin, and Syriac manuscripts, that Irenaeus quoted them as Mark's around 180, more than a century before Sinaiticus and Vaticanus were copied, that Vaticanus's blank column suggests its scribe knew more text, and that ending a book with the word for would be strange.

Among those who think the verses were added, opinion divides again. Some, including R. H. Lightfoot, Andrew Lincoln, and Daniel Wallace, hold that Mark deliberately ended at verse 8, leaving the promise of verse 7 standing and the reader to carry the message the women did not. Others, including Bruce Metzger, Robert Gundry, N. Clayton Croy (The Mutilation of Mark's Gospel, 2003), N. T. Wright, and Keith Elliott, think the original ending was lost, often noting that the outer leaf of a codex is the easiest to lose and that Matthew and Luke, who used Mark, both continue with appearances. This is a second-order question on which faithful Christians disagree. Most modern Bibles print verses 9 to 20 with a note or in brackets. Readers can receive the passage as an ancient and valuable witness to how the early church summarized the resurrection appearances and the mission, while building no doctrine or practice on it alone. The resurrection does not depend on these verses; verses 1 to 8 proclaim it plainly, and the other Gospels and Paul's list of witnesses in 1 Corinthians 15:3-8 tell of the appearances.

hard.q: Can a historian believe the tomb was empty and that Jesus rose?
hard.a:
The objection has several forms, and some are very old. Matthew already reports that the priests spread the story that the disciples stole the body (Matthew 28:11-15), and Justin Martyr says it was still circulating around 160. Celsus, in the second century, dismissed the witnesses as a half-frantic woman and others deceived by dreams or wishes (Origen, Against Celsus 2.55). Hermann Samuel Reimarus (1778) revived the theft theory. Modern critics more often argue that the empty-tomb stories grew later: Mark, the earliest Gospel, if it ends at verse 8, narrates no appearance at all, and the women's silence might even explain why no one had heard of an empty tomb before. Gerd Lüdemann (1994) argued that the resurrection faith began with visions, first Peter's, born of grief and guilt, and that the tomb played no part. Jewish readers have generally held that whatever the disciples experienced, the resurrection did not make Jesus the Messiah, since the messianic age of peace did not come.

Responses come from historians of several convictions. Many note that a story invented in the first century would hardly have made women its first witnesses, when Josephus says women's testimony was not accepted, and that the earliest opponents did not deny the tomb was empty but explained it by theft. Paul's list in 1 Corinthians 15:3-8, which he received and handed on within a few years of the events, speaks of burial and resurrection on the third day and names individual and group witnesses, some of whom were still alive. N. T. Wright (The Resurrection of the Son of God, 2003) argued that the combination of an empty tomb and meetings with the risen Jesus is the only sufficient explanation for why Jews who expected a general resurrection at the end suddenly proclaimed one man raised in the middle of history. Dale Allison (Resurrecting Jesus, 2005), a critical scholar cautious about apologetic arguments, concluded that the tomb was probably found empty and that people did see Jesus after his death, while judging that history alone cannot settle what that means. Pinchas Lapide, an Orthodox Jew, went further, accepting the resurrection as a historical event while not accepting Jesus as Messiah. Historians disagree about how far their discipline can reach in a question like this; the church confesses as a first-order article of faith that Jesus was bodily raised, and it invites the skeptic to weigh the witnesses.

observe: Which women come to the tomb, and where else in chapters 15 and 16 have they appeared? What have they seen?
What three statements does the young man make in verse 6, and what does he tell the women to do in verse 7?
In verses 9 to 14, how many times are the disciples said not to believe, and how does Jesus respond?
interpret: Why do you think the message names ‘His disciples and Peter’? What does Peter's name add after 14:66-72?
If Mark ended his Gospel at verse 8, what might he have meant readers to feel and do? If the ending was lost, what would we lose by reading verse 8 as the last word?
How does the risen Jesus going ahead into Galilee connect with the beginning of the Gospel (1:14-20)?
apply: The women came expecting a corpse and found God had acted first. Where are you worrying about a stone God may already have moved?
The first response to the resurrection was fear and silence. What makes you hesitate to speak of the risen Jesus, and what might it look like to speak anyway?
Jesus sent the disciples out right after rebuking their unbelief. How does that shape the way you think about your own doubts and your calling?
